params.text:
What we mean by safeguarding adults

Safeguarding means protecting an adult's right to live in safety, free from abuse and neglect. As a frontline care worker you are often the person who spends the most time with the people you support, so you are frequently the first to notice that something is wrong. That closeness makes safeguarding a core part of your everyday role, not an occasional extra task.

The Care Act 2014 sets out the legal framework for adult safeguarding in England. It places duties on local authorities and expects everyone who works in care to understand their responsibilities.

Who is an adult at risk?

The Care Act describes an adult at risk as someone aged 18 or over who:

  • has needs for care and support (whether or not the local authority is meeting them);
  • is experiencing, or is at risk of, abuse or neglect; and
  • as a result of those care and support needs is unable to protect themselves from that abuse or neglect.

All three parts have to be present. Someone might have care needs yet be well able to keep themselves safe; someone else may face abuse but have no care needs. It is the combination that makes a person an adult at risk, so the same individual can be at risk in one situation and not in another. When these three points apply, this is often called the section 42 duty, and the local authority must make (or arrange) enquiries.

Your responsibility as a care worker

You are not expected to investigate abuse or to decide whether it definitely happened. Your job is to recognise the signs, respond safely, record what you have seen or been told, and report your concern to the right person without delay. Doing nothing because you are unsure is never the safe option. If you have a concern, it must always be passed on.

params.question: As a care worker, it is your job to investigate the abuse yourself and decide whether it really happened before telling anyone.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. You should never try to investigate or confirm abuse yourself. Recognise it, keep people safe, record the facts and report the concern promptly.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Your role is to recognise, respond, record and report. Investigating is for the local authority and other agencies.

params.question: Under the Care Act 2014, which combination describes an adult at risk?

answers.text: An adult with care and support needs who is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect and cannot protect themselves because of those needs.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. All three elements — care needs, abuse or the risk of it, and being unable to self-protect — must be present together.

answers.text: Any adult over 65, because older people are always vulnerable.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Age alone does not make someone an adult at risk; it depends on care needs and the situation.

answers.text: Any adult who has a disability, whatever their circumstances.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Having a disability does not automatically make a person an adult at risk; the Care Act test still has to be met.

answers.text: An adult who is unhappy with their care but has no care and support needs.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Without care and support needs the Care Act definition is not met, although concerns should still be listened to.
